question: How do symmetries induced jointly by data coordinates, architecture, initialization, and inference determine sample efficiency, finite-width feature learning, and changes in empirical learning-curve slope?

key_findings.claim: The paper formalizes algorithmic invariance of an entire learning procedure, which is weaker and different from a trained predictor being invariant to each transformed input.
key_findings.evidence: A stochastic algorithm is G-invariant when training and testing after one common coordinate transformation produces the same distribution of learned predictions. The text explicitly contrasts this with functional invariance f(gx) = f(x). The proof couples transformed first-layer weights throughout gradient updates rather than proving that an individual network ignores transformations.

key_findings.claim: Under iid Gaussian initialization and the analyzed training rules, the four architecture families carry nested coordinate symmetries that become less spurious as spatial weight sharing and pooling are added.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 4.1 assigns full orthogonal invariance O(3d) to fully connected networks, independent per-pixel color rotations O(3)^d to locally connected networks and infinite-width vector-readout CNNs, and shared color rotation O(3) tensor identity to finite vector-readout CNNs and global-average-pooling CNNs. The proof derives these distributional symmetries from the first layer, Gaussian measure, L2 regularization, and coupled SGD updates.

key_findings.claim: On the CIFAR-10 intervention grid, performance tracks alignment between the data coordinates and the algorithm's symmetry more closely than whether the mismatch is introduced through the model or an invertible data transform.
key_findings.evidence: Ninety combinations vary five coordinate systems, six architectures, and three inference regimes. Figure 2 shows monotonic degradation as transformations or architectures impose larger groups judged incompatible with natural images, and roughly matches a transformed-data GAP system to a clean-data architecture with the corresponding invariance. This is a controlled empirical association, not a general theorem that group dimension determines error.

key_findings.claim: The claimed inference synergy is conditional: larger-learning-rate, weight-decayed SGD improves finite networks mainly when architecture and coordinates are already aligned, while NTK regression can win under severe mismatch.
key_findings.evidence: For clean or shared-color-rotated CIFAR with GAP, VEC, or local pooling, moving from the infinite-width NTK to the stronger finite SGD setting raises accuracy, with a cited GAP change from about 77 to 84 percent. Under larger per-pixel or global spurious transformations, the NTK often beats both finite settings. The experiment bundles learning rate, L2, finite width, and feature learning, so it does not isolate which optimizer mechanism causes the gain.

anchors.section: Spurious symmetries eliminate benefit of SGD

key_findings.claim: Finite width breaks a symmetry of the infinite vector-readout convolutional kernel and correlates with a large non-monotonic generalization benefit on clean CIFAR-10.
key_findings.evidence: Finite VEC networks retain only shared color-rotation invariance, whereas their infinite-width limit equals the more symmetric locally connected kernel. On clean coordinates, test accuracy peaks at finite width and then falls toward or through the NTK level; under independent per-pixel rotations, accuracy instead improves toward the infinite-width result. Output-distance experiments place high-performing small-width VEC closer to GAP and large-width or rotated VEC closer to the infinite kernel.

key_findings.claim: The data-improves-data-efficiency or DIDE effect is an empirical change in fitted learning-curve slope, not a validated scaling law or causal phase-transition estimate.
key_findings.evidence: Clean finite VEC on CIFAR steepens with sample size while replacing SGD by NTK, VEC by LCN, or clean coordinates by per-pixel rotations removes the visual effect. On ImageNet, two six-point line fits show cusps for Mixer or rotated ResNet but an approximately straight power law for clean ResNet. No breakpoint uncertainty, alternative functional form, held-out extrapolation, or statistical test is supplied; the CIFAR extension from 45,000 to 90,000 also introduces left-right augmentation rather than only independent new examples.

key_findings.claim: The proposed relationship between the number of examples needed to overcome a mismatch and the dimension of its symmetry group is speculative numerology rather than a derived bound.
key_findings.evidence: The ImageNet cusp near 200,000 examples is compared with the dimensions of O(3)^d and patch-color groups, and the authors suggest roughly dim(G) extra samples may be required. Only a few selected groups and one image domain are tested; permutation-rotated ImageNet remains below 35 percent, while larger ResNet and EfficientNet models partly close the O(3)^d gap. No theorem connects group dimension to the observed cusp.

key_findings.claim: Several reporting choices bias the finite-network comparisons toward successful-looking runs.
key_findings.evidence: A footnote says some Figure 2 configurations have only one or two successful runs. CIFAR runs are classified as successful when training accuracy reaches at least 95 percent, failed runs can be omitted, and the appendix says the highest test accuracy along training is selected even though a separate validation set exists. Width plots require at least four successful runs but still condition on optimization success.

method.core_idea: Treat data, architecture, and inference as one learning system and diagnose their compatibility through the group of coordinate transformations under which the full randomized training procedure has the same prediction distribution.
method.mechanism: Derive first-layer and kernel invariance groups for fully connected, locally connected, vector-readout convolutional, and pooled convolutional networks; transform all train and test images by fixed shared-color, per-pixel-color, permutation, or full orthogonal maps; compare infinite-width NTK regression with two finite-width SGD regimes; vary width and sample count; and relate performance, output-function distances, and fitted learning-curve slopes to symmetry alignment.
assumptions: Gaussian iid initialization and L2-compatible optimization accurately represent the analyzed algorithmic symmetries.
First-layer coordinate invariance is the dominant relevant symmetry of the full learning system.
Shared color rotations are compatible with natural-image structure, while larger per-pixel and global groups are spurious.
Invertibly transformed CIFAR-10 and ImageNet remain meaningful probes of architecture-coordinate mismatch.
Infinite-width NTK regression is an informative no-feature-learning comparison for finite SGD networks.
MSE-trained eight-layer networks and the chosen learning-rate and weight-decay regimes isolate broadly relevant effects.
Piecewise power-law line fits summarize changes in data efficiency.
Image classification findings transfer conceptually to other data modalities, architectures, and inference procedures.

techniques.role: Defines invariance of the randomized training-and-prediction procedure under common coordinate changes.
Couples transformed first-layer weights through SGD to derive architecture-specific symmetry groups.
Applies fixed invertible orthogonal or permutation transformations to every train and test image.
Contrasts infinite-width kernel regression with finite-width feature-learning networks.
Tests symmetry breaking and non-monotonic generalization as convolutional width grows.
Fits log-log learning-curve segments before and after a visually identified cusp.
Measures squared differences between ensemble predictions to locate finite VEC between GAP and its infinite kernel.

evaluations.setting: CIFAR-10 across five coordinate systems, FCN, LCN, VEC, two local-pooling variants and GAP, and NTK or two finite SGD regimes.
evaluations.result: Accuracy degrades with larger architecture-coordinate mismatch, and strong finite SGD helps mainly for aligned convolutional systems.
evaluations.baseline: The clean-data GAP system within each inference regime and the corresponding NTK predictors.

evaluations.setting: Clean or independently color-rotated CIFAR-10 with vector-readout CNN width swept dyadically.
evaluations.metric: Test accuracy and run-to-run variation relative to the infinite-width VEC kernel.
evaluations.result: Clean-data accuracy peaks at finite width then declines, whereas rotated-data accuracy approaches the infinite-width level as width grows.
evaluations.baseline: VEC-infinity, small-learning-rate SGD, and larger-learning-rate plus L2 SGD.

evaluations.setting: CIFAR-10 sample size from 320 through 45,000 and a 90,000-example augmented endpoint.
evaluations.metric: Log-log test error or MSE learning curves.
evaluations.result: Only clean finite VEC with SGD shows the headline steepening; replacing data, model, or inference removes it.
evaluations.baseline: Per-pixel-rotated VEC, clean LCN, and infinite VEC with NTK.

evaluations.setting: ImageNet subsets for ResNet101 or a small MLP-Mixer on clean or per-pixel-color-rotated coordinates.
evaluations.metric: Top-1 error and slopes from two six-point log-log fits.
evaluations.result: Clean ResNet is close to one power law; the other three curves show a visual cusp and later slopes that approach the clean ResNet slope.
evaluations.baseline: Clean ResNet101 trained with the same SGD code.

evaluations.setting: ResNet and EfficientNet family scaling on clean, independently color-rotated, or pixel-permuted ImageNet.
evaluations.metric: Top-1 accuracy gap and learning dynamics.
evaluations.result: Larger models narrow the independent-color-rotation gap, reportedly to roughly one percent for the largest EfficientNet, but permutation-rotated test accuracy remains below 35 percent for tested ResNets.

evaluations.setting: Continuous paths from clean to independently color-rotated CIFAR and widths 64 through 512.
evaluations.metric: Ensemble output distance to GAP and infinite VEC plus test accuracy.
evaluations.result: Increasing rotation or width moves finite VEC predictions toward the infinite VEC solution and away from GAP while accuracy falls.
evaluations.baseline: Ten-initialization ensemble predictions from GAP and VEC-infinity.

limitations: Author-stated: the analysis uses prototypical architectures and each more complex architecture requires a case-specific symmetry derivation.
Author-stated: later layers can contribute additional invariances not captured by the first-layer analysis.
Author-stated: permutation-group analogies under non-Gaussian initialization need more rigorous experiments.
Author-stated: exact finite-width Bayesian inference is unavailable, so the inference comparison substitutes NTK or NNGP limits.
Reviewer inference: choosing the highest test accuracy along training leaks test information into model selection.
Reviewer inference: discarding optimization failures and reporting some settings from only one or two successful runs creates survivor bias.
Reviewer inference: the stronger SGD condition changes learning rate and L2 simultaneously, so the source of improvement is not isolated.

Reviewer inference: the NTK comparison also replaces finite VEC with its infinite-width kernel, so it jointly changes feature learning, width, and the effective symmetry group rather than isolating inference alone.
Reviewer inference: calling O(3) tensor identity the largest data-compatible group is based on visual and task performance judgments, not an estimated invariance of the true distribution.
Reviewer inference: the DIDE cusp and dim(G) sample heuristic have no uncertainty, formal model comparison, or prospective scaling test.
Reviewer inference: the 90,000-example CIFAR point introduces augmentation, confounding quantity of independent data with an additional invariance intervention.
Reviewer inference: ImageNet models are trained for a fixed 150 epochs, so increasing sample count also increases the number of optimizer updates and total training compute.
Reviewer inference: output S-distance varies with width and coordinate mismatch but is associational; it does not identify symmetry change as the causal source of accuracy differences.
Reviewer inference: all evidence is image classification with fixed invertible coordinate distortions; it does not show a general resolution of the curse of dimensionality.
Reviewer inference: algorithmic invariance in distribution does not say that a single trained model is functionally invariant or robust.
failure_modes: A practitioner hard-codes an approximate symmetry that discards a weak but label-relevant direction and loses irrecoverable accuracy.
A learned finite network appears symmetry-breaking only because failed or poorly optimized seeds were removed.
Test-set checkpoint selection inflates the apparent benefit of one width or optimizer regime.
A visual learning-curve bend is fit as two power laws but disappears with denser sampling, alternate loss, or prospective data.
An invertible coordinate transformation preserves Bayes information yet creates an architecture-specific optimization barrier mistaken for intrinsic data complexity.
A larger model partially memorizes a fixed coordinate distortion without learning the intended natural symmetry.
The relevant symmetry acts in deeper representations or outputs, while a first-layer input-group audit misses it.
A symmetry-discovery method returns a superset of the true group and imposes a harmful invariance.
reusable_insights: Audit data coordinates, architecture, initialization, optimizer, regularization, and augmentation as one system rather than assigning performance to architecture alone.
Keep algorithmic invariance, representation equivariance, functional invariance, and data-distribution symmetry conceptually separate.
Use invertible coordinate interventions to test whether an inductive bias exploits structure rather than information content.
Finite width can remove an undesirable infinite-kernel symmetry, so wider is not automatically a cleaner approximation to useful feature learning.
Symmetry benefits should be measured against approximately symmetric and symmetry-violating targets, not only perfectly constructed cases.
Scaling-law claims need prospective held-out sample sizes, breakpoint uncertainty, and alternative curve families.
Report all seeds, failed-run rates, validation-selected checkpoints, and matched optimizer ablations when studying feature-learning synergy.
open_questions: Can the relevant algorithmic symmetry group of a modern transformer, optimizer, augmentation pipeline, and tokenizer be computed or estimated end to end?
What finite-time mechanism moves vector-readout CNNs from an LCN-like function toward a pooled solution?
Can one predict the best degree of approximate equivariance when the data symmetry is imperfect?
Does the DIDE cusp replicate prospectively on new sample sizes, modalities, losses, and independently collected data?
Is there any rigorous relation between symmetry-group complexity and examples required to overcome a mismatched inductive bias?
How can unknown symmetries be discovered without collapsing label-relevant rare exceptions?
Which optimizer properties preserve, break, or learn symmetries beyond those imposed by initialization?
Can output-distance and learned-group diagnostics distinguish useful symmetry breaking from memorization of a fixed coordinate transform?

competitive_landscape.title: Why Are Convolutional Nets More Sample-Efficient than Fully-Connected Nets?
competitive_landscape.difference: Li, Zhang, and Arora prove a natural task with an O(1) versus Omega(d squared) sample gap by exploiting the orthogonal equivariance of Gaussian-initialized gradient methods. Xiao and Pennington generalize the diagnostic to several CNN readouts, transformed image data, finite versus infinite width, and learning-curve interactions, but their broad empirical group-dimension story is less rigorous than this predecessor's constructed lower bound.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning with invariances in random features and kernel models
competitive_landscape.difference: Mei, Misiakiewicz, and Montanari derive a d-to-the-alpha sample and feature saving for invariant random features and kernels and show when data augmentation matches an invariant estimator. The present paper focuses on mismatch and feature-learning departures from infinite kernels on real image benchmarks rather than a high-dimensional risk theorem.

competitive_landscape.title: Data-driven emergence of convolutional structure in neural networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Ingrosso and Goldt analytically and numerically show localized, space-tiling receptive fields emerging from higher-order local image statistics in an initially fully connected model. That work offers a concrete pattern-formation mechanism for learning convolutional structure, whereas DIDE infers a function-class transition primarily from performance and output distances.

competitive_landscape.title: Approximately Equivariant Networks for Imperfectly Symmetric Dynamics
competitive_landscape.difference: Wang, Walters, and Yu relax exact equivariance for dynamics whose symmetries are only approximate, directly targeting the risk that an overly large hard-coded group is spurious. Xiao and Pennington diagnose harmful mismatch but do not train an adaptive continuum between invariant and unrestricted models.

competitive_landscape.title: Equivariance with Learned Canonicalization Functions
competitive_landscape.difference: Kaba and colleagues learn a canonical representative before an ordinary backbone, offering exact equivariance without constraining every layer to a specialized architecture. This is a practical response to the data-model compatibility problem, although it assumes the target group is known and does not address DIDE scaling.

competitive_landscape.title: Generative Adversarial Symmetry Discovery
competitive_landscape.difference: LieGAN adversarially learns continuous equivariances from data and then transfers them into equivariant models, replacing manual group choice with an empirical discovery procedure. It tackles an operational gap left here, but learned transformations still require checks that they preserve labels and rare exceptions rather than only marginal data appearance.

competitive_landscape.title: Efficient Learning and Symmetry Discovery under Exact Invariances
competitive_landscape.difference: Soleymani and colleagues give polynomial-time algorithms and sample guarantees for exact known invariances and recover unknown finite-group symmetries under their regression assumptions. This provides a sharper computational and statistical target than the present paper's heuristic group-dimension explanation, while covering a much more restricted exact-invariance setting than natural images.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Understanding deep-learning sample efficiency requires treating data, model, and inference as an integrated system; compatible symmetries enable SGD and finite-width gains, while additional data can trigger a more efficient function class.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper proves distributional invariance groups for four architecture families, runs a 90-cell CIFAR intervention grid, identifies finite-width vector-CNN symmetry breaking, and presents CIFAR and ImageNet learning curves with mismatch ablations.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The valuable contribution is an unusually concrete experimental calculus for architecture-coordinate-optimizer compatibility and the observation that an infinite-width limit can restore a harmful symmetry. Orthogonal-algorithm lower bounds and invariant-kernel sample gains already established the central sample-efficiency mechanism. DIDE is an intriguing descriptive hypothesis, but test-set checkpointing, omitted failures, mixed interventions, visually chosen cusps, and speculative dim(G) matching mean it is not yet a scaling law or an explanation of how deep learning breaks the curse of dimensionality in general.
